\chapter{Four Words on the Face}
\label{ch:ka-face-words}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my eye, ear, nose and mouth in Kannada, and say which of the four the Dravidian family agrees on closely and which one splits.}

Name \kn{ಕಣ್ಣು}, \kn{ಕಿವಿ}, \kn{ಮೂಗು} and \kn{ಬಾಯಿ}, and finally explain \kn{ಬಾಯಿ} — the word this book already used twice, unglossed, as proof of the v $\to$ b law behind \kn{ಬಾ} and \kn{ಬರೆ}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kaṇṇu]{\kn{ಕಣ್ಣು} (kaṇṇu) — \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} the same word across four languages}

\label{lesson:KA-C37-kannu}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Tale}, \emph{kai} — Chapter 13's head and hand, and nothing more of the body since. This chapter adds four words to that short list, starting above the nose.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಕಣ್ಣು}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಕಣ್ಣು}} — \emph{kaṇṇu} — \textbf{eye}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಕಣ್ಣು}.} — \emph{nanna kaṇṇu.} — \textquotedblleft{}My eye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಕಣ್ಣು}} continues Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*kaṇ}, \textquotedblleft{}eye.\textquotedblright{} Tamil \textbf{\ta{கண்}} (\emph{kaṇ}) and Malayalam \textbf{\ml{കണ്ണ്}} (\emph{kaṇṇŭ}) sit close beside it — and Telugu \textbf{\te{కన్ను}} (\emph{kannu}) sits closest of all, nearly identical letter for letter. Four languages that otherwise pull apart on nearly everything — tense, the \emph{p} $\to$ \emph{h} law, half their vocabulary — agree almost completely on this one, the same closeness the last chapter found between Kannada's \emph{magaḷu} and Tamil and Malayalam's own \emph{makaḷ}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nanna kaṇṇu\textquotedblright{} — my eye
  \item the four sisters, nearly one word — \textquotedblleft{}kaṇṇu … kaṇ … kaṇṇŭ … kannu\textquotedblright{}
  \item two more near-matches — \textquotedblleft{}magaḷu, makaḷ … kaṇṇu, kaṇ\textquotedblright{}
  \item three body words now — \textquotedblleft{}tale, kai, kaṇṇu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my eye.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nanna kaṇṇu}.) Which sister matches Kannada's word almost exactly? (\textbf{Telugu} — \emph{kannu}.) Which earlier word showed this same closeness with Tamil and Malayalam? (\emph{\textbf{\kn{ಮಗಳು}}}, \emph{magaḷu}.) Name the body words you have now. (\emph{Tale}, head; \emph{kai}, hand; \emph{kaṇṇu}, eye.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kivi]{\kn{ಕಿವಿ} (kivi) — \textquotedblleft{}ear,\textquotedblright{} where Tamil's everyday word actually diverges}

\label{lesson:KA-C37-kivi}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Kaṇṇu} matched all three sisters closely. This one is honest about matching only some of them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಕಿವಿ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಕಿವಿ}} — \emph{kivi} — \textbf{ear}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಕಿವಿ}.} — \emph{nanna kivi.} — \textquotedblleft{}My ear.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಕಿವಿ}} continues Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*kewi}, \textquotedblleft{}ear.\textquotedblright{} Telugu's everyday word \textbf{\te{చెవి}} (\emph{cevi}) is the same root, and so is Tamil's — but only in its \textbf{literary} register: \textbf{\ta{செவி}} (\emph{cevi}) shows up in poetry and formal speech, while ordinary spoken Tamil reaches for an unrelated word instead, \textbf{\ta{காது}} (\emph{kātu}). It is the same honest split Chapter 34 found in \textbf{\ta{கேள்}}/\emph{kēḷ} against Telugu's \emph{vinu} and \emph{aḍugu}: a shared root can go on living in one register of a language while everyday speech moves on to something else.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nanna kivi\textquotedblright{} — my ear
  \item the shared root's two lives — \textquotedblleft{}cevi, literary … kātu, everyday\textquotedblright{}
  \item eye, then ear — \textquotedblleft{}kaṇṇu … kivi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my ear.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nanna kivi}.) Does everyday spoken Tamil use the same root as \emph{kivi}? (\textbf{No} — it uses \emph{kātu}; the shared root \emph{cevi} survives mostly in literary Tamil.) Which earlier Kannada word split the same way? (\emph{\textbf{\ta{கேள்}}}/\emph{kēḷu} — kept by three sisters, dropped in Telugu's everyday speech.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mūgu]{\kn{ಮೂಗು} (mūgu) — \textquotedblleft{}nose,\textquotedblright{} where Telugu is the one that drifts}

\label{lesson:KA-C37-moogu}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Kivi} split the family down a register line. This word splits it a different way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮೂಗು}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಮೂಗು}} — \emph{mūgu} — \textbf{nose}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಮೂಗು}.} — \emph{nanna mūgu.} — \textquotedblleft{}My nose.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಮೂಗು}} continues Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*mūnk(k)u}, \textquotedblleft{}nose.\textquotedblright{} Tamil \textbf{\ta{மூக்கு}} (\emph{mūkku}) and Malayalam \textbf{\ml{മൂക്ക്}} (\emph{mūkkŭ}) sit close beside Kannada's own form. Telugu is the outlier this round: \textbf{\te{ముక్కు}} (\emph{mukku}) is treated as a slightly irregular reflex, likely blended with a separate word for \textquotedblleft{}face.\textquotedblright{} Ear put Telugu with the group and split Tamil's registers; nose does the opposite — Telugu drifts, and Tamil and Malayalam hold the line.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nanna mūgu\textquotedblright{} — my nose
  \item the close sisters, then the drifting one — \textquotedblleft{}mūkku, mūkkŭ … mukku\textquotedblright{}
  \item ear, then nose — \textquotedblleft{}kivi … mūgu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my nose.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nanna mūgu}.) Which sister drifts from the shared root this time? (\textbf{Telugu} — \emph{mukku}, likely blended with its word for \textquotedblleft{}face.\textquotedblright{}) Which two sisters hold the root closely? (\textbf{Tamil and Malayalam} — \emph{mūkku}, \emph{mūkkŭ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bāyi]{\kn{ಬಾಯಿ} (bāyi) — \textquotedblleft{}mouth,\textquotedblright{} a word you've already met twice}

\label{lesson:KA-C37-baayi}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Bā}, come; \emph{bare}, write. Both chapters used one more word in passing, to prove the same sound law, and neither one told you what it meant.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬಾಯಿ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಬಾಯಿ}} — \emph{bāyi} — \textbf{mouth}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಬಾಯಿ}.} — \emph{nanna bāyi.} — \textquotedblleft{}My mouth.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Four body words now: \emph{tale}, \emph{kai}, \emph{kaṇṇu}, \emph{kivi}, \emph{mūgu}, \emph{bāyi} — six.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಬಾಯಿ}} answers Tamil \textbf{\ta{வாய்}} (\emph{vāy}), \textquotedblleft{}mouth,\textquotedblright{} through the exact law Chapter 32 gave you: word-initial Tamil \emph{v-} becomes Kannada \emph{b-}. You have already seen this pair once, sitting quietly inside Chapter 32's etymology note for \textbf{\kn{ಬಾ}}, and again inside Chapter 33's for \textbf{\kn{ಬರೆ}} — both times as a worked example, neither time explained. Here is what it means:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Tamil} & \textbf{Kannada} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
\emph{vā} & \emph{bā} & come \\
\emph{varai} & \emph{bare} & write, draw \\
\emph{vāy} & \emph{bāyi} & mouth \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three clean proofs of one law, and this lesson finally cashes in the third.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nanna bāyi\textquotedblright{} — my mouth
  \item the three proofs — \textquotedblleft{}vā, bā … varai, bare … vāy, bāyi\textquotedblright{}
  \item all six body words — \textquotedblleft{}tale, kai, kaṇṇu, kivi, mūgu, bāyi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my mouth.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nanna bāyi}.) Which two earlier chapters already used this exact word, without explaining it? (\textbf{Chapter 32's} \emph{bā} note and \textbf{Chapter 33's} \emph{bare} note.) Give the law it proves, and its other two examples. (\textbf{Word-initial \emph{v-} becomes \emph{b-}} — \emph{vā} $\to$ \emph{bā}, \emph{varai} $\to$ \emph{bare}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
